b: Enhanced dynamic allocation (EDA) is a feature of Google's publisher ad server that allowed bids from Google's ad exchange to compete for impressions a publisher had already reserved for guaranteed, directly sold campaigns. Before it, booked campaigns took the impressions they needed and the exchange saw what was left. EDA replaced that rule with a price test. The ad server assigned each guaranteed line item a temporary value for a given impression, and if an exchange buyer offered more, the exchange won that impression while the direct campaign was steered toward later ones. Litigation now asks whom that test really served.

The feature lives inside Google Ad Manager, previously DoubleClick for Publishers (DFP), which Google acquired with DoubleClick in 2008. Every ad request is matched against line items, the ad server's records of what is booked to run where, and each line item type carries a priority number in which lower numbers win. Google's delivery documentation places "Sponsorship and Standard line items" in "the priority range of 1 to 10". These are the guaranteed types, sold at an agreed price with a delivery promise. Remnant line items, the non-guaranteed Network, Bulk and Price Priority types, sit at priority 12 and compete on price. Google restricted each type to a defined purpose from May 1, 2020.

Plain dynamic allocation, the older mechanism, arrived with the DoubleClick Ad Exchange (AdX) on September 18, 2009. It let a live AdX bid beat a booked remnant line item when the bid was higher. The UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), in an appendix to its December 2019 interim report on online platforms and digital advertising, described how this worked: the ad server took the price of the highest booked remnant line item and used it as the floor for AdX. Guaranteed campaigns stayed outside that contest.

The CMA put the change in one sentence: "In 2014, Google introduced Enhanced Dynamic Allocation, which extended the principle of dynamic allocation to 'guaranteed line items'." AdX bids, and other exchanges' estimated bids, could win an impression "if they were sufficiently high" and if winning would not cause the direct deal to under-deliver, according to the CMA.

Google's documentation describes the logic without the EDA label. Guaranteed line items compete using "a temporary CPM or 'opportunity cost' that Ad Manager calculates automatically", and Open Auction or remnant demand serves "if they pay more than the opportunity cost of not serving" the guaranteed line item. CPM, cost per mille, is the price of one thousand impressions.
The sequence for a single impression runs roughly as follows:

Eligibility. The ad server identifies every Standard and remnant line item that could serve the impression. Standard line items with a fixed impression goal can be included. Sponsorship line items set to take 100% of an inventory slice fall outside the calculation, a point Google's expert Paul Milgrom made in the New York litigation.

Temporary price. For an eligible Standard line item, the ad server computes a temporary CPM from its priority, its delivery progress and historical bid data. A campaign behind schedule gets a higher temporary price, according to MonetizeMore, a publisher yield consultancy, writing in January 2016.
Exchange test. The higher of that figure and the best remnant CPM is passed to AdX as its floor. If an AdX buyer clears it, the exchange serves. If not, the guaranteed or remnant line item does.

An illustration: a publisher sells a Standard campaign at $20 CPM for one million impressions over 30 days. Halfway through the month the campaign is on pace, so the ad server might value the next impression at $6, well below the $20 contract price, because the campaign can easily pick up a later impression instead. A remnant line item sits at $4. The floor sent to AdX is $6. An AdX buyer bidding $9 takes the impression. The direct advertiser still receives its million impressions, but not necessarily this one.

Publishers do not see the inputs. Glenn Berntson, a Google engineering director, testified in the Virginia remedies proceedings in 2025 that EDA draws on a seven-day window of bid data, recalculated daily in a job taking roughly 10 hours across 4,000 computers, as PPC Land's publisher ad server explainer records.

The documentation now groups this behaviour under dynamic allocation and a network-level switch called optimized competition, found under Admin, Global settings and Network settings. When dynamic allocation sets "a very high temporary CPM to protect the delivery of an Ad Manager standard line item", optimized competition can set a different price, which "is always at least as high as the CPM of the competing Ad Manager standard line item" and is "algorithmically determined per query", according to Google. It "does not change the price for sponsorship line items", and Google acknowledges that activating it "may impact standard line item reservation delivery".

The surrounding rules kept moving. Header bidding spread from 2015; Google rolled out Exchange Bidding to all DFP publishers in April 2018, and unified pricing rules, announced in May 2019, stopped publishers setting higher floors for AdX than for rivals, ahead of a unified first-price auction that September.

Direct sales are usually a publisher's best-priced inventory. EDA put a machine-set price on those impressions and opened them to an exchange owned by the company running the ad server. For advertisers buying direct, the impressions their campaign received were the ones exchange buyers had passed over.

That is the core of the private damages claims. On September 30, 2026, Judge P. Kevin Castel in New York refused to end the Gannett and Daily Mail suits and found that "a reasonable jury could find that EDA caused antitrust injury". The opinion quotes an internal Google description of EDA as a way to "cherry-pick higher revenue impressions while respecting the delivery constraints", and a September 2016 email stating: "with EDA on we set the reserve price at $1, and any AdX buyer including GDN can win." GDN is the Google Display Network.

Ali Hortacsu, the publishers' economist at the University of Chicago, estimated that EDA reduced the global value of direct sales by approximately 24.1%. His EDA damages for Gannett are $348.9 million in the US and $434.8 million worldwide, against a total Gannett claim of $900.77 million, as PPC Land reported when Castel sent the damages claims to a jury. Einer Elhauge, for the AdX advertiser class, credits EDA with raising AdX revenue by more than $250 million a year.

The first criticism is cream-skimming. Because the temporary price could sit below the contracted price, plaintiffs argue, AdX could take the most valuable impressions "no matter how high the direct price".

The second is self-preferencing. Li, an economist for the plaintiffs, concluded that EDA "gave publishers no choice about which exchanges could bid on direct-deal inventory", advantaged AdX over third-party exchanges, and "probabilistically throttled" bidders arriving through header bidding. The same 2016 email chain said rivals "cannot compete with AdX through EDA on the similar footing". The CMA had noted that dynamic allocation gave AdX "an advantage that other SSPs considered unfair", SSPs being supply-side platforms.

The third is opacity. Plaintiffs cite evidence that EDA's functions "remained unknown until revealed by government investigations in or around 2020" and that it "was not widely understood even within Google". Castel held that this could support tolling the limitations period.

Google contests each point. Milgrom argued that publishers could have recreated the pre-EDA order with price floors, placed direct deals in 100% Sponsorship line items, or switched off dynamic allocation for chosen exchanges. Google argued that Gannett could have cut its EDA damages by $191.4 million, and told the court that it no longer uses EDA, dynamic allocation or dynamic revenue share. Its Help Center pages, as of October 2026, still document dynamic allocation, temporary CPMs and optimized competition, and the record reviewed does not reconcile the two. None of these points are findings; Castel left them to a jury.
Dynamic allocation. The 2009 mechanism let AdX outbid booked remnant line items. EDA, from 2014, extended the contest to guaranteed Standard line items.
Optimized competition. A current Ad Manager setting that adjusts the price non-guaranteed demand must beat against Standard line items, documented under its own name.

First look and last look. First look gave AdX the first chance to buy an impression; last look let it bid after seeing rival prices. Both concern sequencing between exchanges, while EDA concerns competition between exchanges and direct deals.
Programmatic guaranteed. Programmatic guaranteed deals sell reserved inventory to a named buyer through automated pipes, with no auction.

On September 2, 2026, Judge Leonie Brinkema in Virginia declined to order a sale of AdX and imposed six years of worldwide conduct rules, banning first look and last look on open-web display inventory and requiring unified pricing rules to be deprecated. PPC Land's coverage of the order does not record any provision naming EDA, and EDA was not among the Virginia findings Castel gave preclusive effect, so it must be proved afresh. Castel deferred the AdX class's request for an injunction against EDA to the Virginia remedies.

On October 2, 2026 the Department of Justice, 17 states and Google returned a single 41-page proposed final judgment, the government seeking AdX access for Prebid within six months and Google asking for twelve. As of late November 2026, no signed final judgment had been reported. In New York, the Gannett and Daily Mail trial first set for April 2027 has been pushed to October 25, 2027, according to MLex. Teads, in a complaint citing 6.88 trillion impressions lost by rival exchanges, treats dynamic allocation as a routing advantage. A feature built to fill direct deals more profitably has become one of the costliest entries in Google's litigation docket.

Who. Google built and operated enhanced dynamic allocation inside DFP, now Google Ad Manager. Publishers' ad operations teams and direct sales teams were affected on the sell side; AdX buyers, including Google's own Display Network, gained access on the buy side. Gannett, the Daily Mail, the AdX advertiser class and their economists, along with Google's expert Paul Milgrom, are the main parties disputing its effects.

What. A feature that assigned guaranteed Standard line items a machine-calculated temporary CPM per impression and let AdX win any impression where a buyer beat that price, provided the direct campaign stayed on pace.

When. Introduced in 2014, five years after plain dynamic allocation launched with AdX in September 2009. Its mechanics became public mainly through government investigations from around 2020, and a New York judge allowed EDA claims to proceed toward a jury on September 30, 2026, with trial now set for October 2027.
Where. Inside the publisher ad server, at the point where guaranteed reservations, remnant line items and exchange demand are compared for each ad request on open-web display inventory.

Why. Google's documentation frames dynamic allocation as raising revenue "without compromising the performance of guaranteed line item delivery". Plaintiffs argue it skimmed the most valuable direct-sold impressions for AdX at prices below contract rates, disadvantaged rival exchanges and stayed opaque for years. Those claims remain allegations pending trial.
